steps.prompt_exact: I want a tiny puzzle-box escape game I can open as one HTML file: three compact rooms, clickable objects, clue-driven inventory, and a final lock that feels fair instead of random.
steps.response_exact:
Check frontend-design skill for any relevant guidance before building a complex interactive HTML fileCheck frontend-design skill for any relevant guidance before building a complex interactive HTML fileThis is going to be a standalone HTML file — a proper self-contained artifact, not an inline widget. Let me build it.Ran a command, created a file, read a fileRan a command, created a file, read a fileThe Archivist's Study — open that HTML file in any browser and you're good to go.
Here's how it plays, without being a walkthrough:
Three rooms — the Study, the Walled Garden, and the Library — each connected by door buttons. You navigate freely, no fixed order required.
Click to investigate. Every clickable object responds with flavor text in the Inspection panel. Takeable items (a journal, a brass key, a faded letter) drop into your Inventory sidebar, where you can re-read them anytime. Clues auto-log into the Notes panel so you're never hunting back through inspection text.
The final lock is a 3-dial combination. The three digits are each derived from a different room:
Dial I comes from the Study
Dial II from the Garden
Dial III requires cross-referencing information from two rooms
No digit is arbitrary — every answer is explicitly clued at least twice (once to discover it, once in the library to confirm the format). If you miss anything, the placard in Room 3 restates the full logic structure without giving the numbers.
Quality-of-life touches:
After 3 failed lock attempts, directional hints fire ("Dial II is too high")
Event log in the corner tracks what just happened
Win screen shows your move count, items found, and lock attempts
Fully restartable with no page reload
Escape roomCode · HTML Download

steps.prompt_exact: This first version is playable, but the help/reset pieces are too hidden while you are still inside the puzzle. Add a small Hint button with staged nudges, a Reset button that restarts without reloading the page, and keep the room/object controls comfortable for phone taps.

Hint button in the header — staged nudges per room keyed to what you've discovered so far
Reset button in the header — instant in-place restart, no reload

Hint button — staged nudges, not giveaways. The 💡 Hint button lives right in the header. Inside, there are up to four nudge stages, but they unlock progressively — you can only see the next stage after your notes show you've actually discovered the relevant clue. Mobile tap targets. Object buttons, door buttons, inventory items, and lock dial controls all hit 44–52px minimum height. The dial up/down arrows are larger and centered. steps.prompt_exact: The reset bug is still there: after opening Hint, pressing Reset leaves the hint overlay visible. Make reset close every overlay reliably, and add a Reset button inside the hint overlay too so the player can restart without first closing the hint panel. Keep the clue-progress strip spoiler-free and add one short line that explains it.
steps.response_exact:
Viewed 2 filesViewed 2 filesFound it. The display: none / display: flex toggle via .open class is the problem — classList.remove('open') works, but only if the element actually has display: none as its base state. The confirm overlay sits at z-index: 120 on top, and when the player goes Hint → Reset → confirm "Reset", doReset() is called while the confirm overlay also still has open on it. But the deeper issue is that the hint overlay uses display: none as default, yet after opening the confirm overlay on top, the z-ordering means the hint overlay's .open class removal appears to not work visually if something is re-rendering in between. Let me check the confirm path fully.Viewed 2 filesViewed 2 filesGot it. The actual bug: hint-overlay has no inline style on it in the HTML, so its base display state is the browser default (block for a div), not none. The CSS rule #hint-overlay { display: none; } only applies when the stylesheet loads — but classList.remove('open') only removes the class; it doesn't force display: none back if the base CSS rule gets bypassed. The safe fix is to toggle display directly via style, not rely on class-only toggling for all overlays. I'll also:
Switch all three overlays to use style.display directly — bulletproof across all paths
Add a Reset button inside the hint overlay
Add the explanatory line for the progress strip
Check progress strip HTML to find where to add the explanatory lineCheck progress strip HTML to find where to add the explanatory lineNow I have everything I need. Making all three targeted changes:Viewed 2 files, edited a fileViewed 2 files, edited a fileGood. Now remove the two remaining .open CSS rules for lock and confirm (they're no longer used — visibility will be set via style.display directly):Edited 2 filesEdited 2 filesNow rewrite doReset, confirmReset, closeConfirm, openLock, closeLock, openHint, closeHint to all use style.display directly:Edited 3 filesEdited 3 filesAlso fix tryLock's win path which still calls classList.remove:Fix tryLock win path to use style.displayFix tryLock win path to use style.displayNow add the Reset button inside the hint overlay and the progress strip explanatory line:Edited 2 filesEdited 2 filesNow add the explanatory line to the progress strip:Add a short caption line below the progress strip cells explaining what it showsAdd a short caption line below the progress strip cells explaining what it showsAdd the caption CSS:Add CSS for the progress strip caption lineAdd CSS for the progress strip caption lineVerify no .open class usage remains for overlays, and check the final reset + hint functions look right:Confirm no .open class toggling remains and all display control is via style.displayConfirm no .open class toggling remains and all display control is via style.displayZero .open class toggles left — every overlay is controlled purely by style.display. Quick sanity check on the hint footer HTML:Confirm hint footer, reset button, and caption elements are all in placeConfirm hint footer, reset button, and caption elements are all in placeEverything is in order.Presented filePresented fileThree changes, each with a clear reason:
Root cause of the reset bug fixed. The previous version controlled overlay visibility by adding/removing a CSS .open class that toggled display: flex. That's fragile when overlays are stacked — classList.remove('open') strips the class, but the browser's computed display can get out of sync with what CSS expects when multiple overlays are active at the same time. Every overlay now uses element.style.display = 'none' / 'flex' directly. Inline styles always win over stylesheet rules, so doReset() closing them is unconditional regardless of what state the DOM is in.
Reset button inside the hint panel. A small ↺ Reset button sits in the hint overlay's footer, right-aligned next to the stage counter. It calls confirmReset() — same confirm dialog, same doReset() path — so the player can restart from inside the hint panel without a detour through close → header → reset.
Progress strip caption. One short italic line sits immediately below the strip: "Each dot fills when you've found that dial's clue source — not the digit itself." It's below the cells so it doesn't compete with the labels, and it's sized small enough to read as an aside rather than a heading. Spoiler-safety is unchanged — the conditions that light each dot require finding the source note (clock examined, rose bed found, both birth year and retirement year in notes), never the digit value.Escape roomCode · HTML Download
